intro_en:
The Israel National Trail completes its crossing of the eastern Ramon area and descends to the Arava. The descent and the transition to the Arava also affect the weather: this is a region with low annual rainfall and a high average temperature, which is clearly reflected in the landscape and the vegetation.

 Nahal Gevanim - Gev Holit (44)
 Sapir - Tzukim (46)
character_en: Ascents and descents, some of them steep
transport_en: At the end point: in the village of Sapir or on the Arava Road at the turn-off to Sapir
pois_en: Nahal Nekarot. Har Yahav. Nahal Tzvira. "The Cracks". The caldera
important_en: Vehicle access to the Gev Holit overnight campsite is possible only with an off-road vehicle.
There is no water source at the campsite. It is recommended to consider water caching at the campsite.
Drinking water and a proper campsite are available at the Be'erot campground, about 3 km along an easy road from the Nahal Gevanim campsite.
Mobile phone reception is problematic in the western part of the segment.
description_en:
The segment begins at the Gev Holit overnight campsite, at an elevation of 150 metres, and from there leads down to the Arava and on to the end point at Sapir, which lies at sea level.
From the campsite we head out into Nahal Nekarot. Its wide channel testifies to the long way it has travelled from its source. More than that, it testifies to the size of the area it drains. Nahal Nekarot is one of the largest streams in the country: it is about 60 km long and its drainage basin covers about 1,000 square km. At this point, where Nahal Kamai enters Nahal Nekarot, the drainage of the entire Ramon Crater is complete.
The channel is carpeted with pebbles and rock debris that are very noticeable underfoot. We walk along a red-marked road that comes in from the direction of the Arava Road, from Ein Yahav, through the Nekarot channel to the campsite.
We turn right onto a blue-marked footpath branching off the road. A sign for identifying the fork: it is in the area where the road approaches the right bank, towards a rocky spur descending from Har Yahav.
The Israel National Trail skirts Har Yahav from the north, at the foot of the spurs descending to the Nekarot channel. The trail crosses small tributaries coming down from the mountain. When we reach a larger tributary in which several acacia trees grow, the trail turns south towards the ascent of Har Yahav. Ahead of us is a dry waterfall, which we bypass on the right, and we continue walking beside the channel. The plateau of Har Yahav is ringed by a cliff that looks like a crown on its head. A spur descending from the back of the plateau breaks the cliff line and lets the trail climb to the plateau on a relatively gentle ascent.
On the plateau, at the end of the climb, the Israel National Trail turns left towards the south-west. But first it is worth taking in the view from Har Yahav over its surroundings. Looking back towards the ascent of the mountain, we see the lower course of the Nahal Nekarot channel on its way to the Arava, winding in the shape of the letter S. Above and to the left of the distant bend, we can make out a saddle: this is "Anmar's Knife" (Sakin Anmar), a very narrow saddle squeezed between two bends of two channels.
North of the saddle is the channel of Nahal Anmar, which cannot be seen from the viewpoint, and south of the saddle is the Nekarot channel, in plain view. In the future, geological changes are expected to cause the saddle to be "eaten away" from both sides by the two streams, and stream capture will occur (on a topographic map you can clearly see the narrow saddle between two stream bends, shaped like this: >|< ).
To look west towards the area through which segment 43 passes, walk a short distance to the right along the edge of the plateau. There you can see Nahal Nekarot arriving from the south. To the right of the Nekarot channel, on the skyline, stands Har Badad. Opposite is the channel of Nahal Kamai, which comes in from the west and joins the wide channel of Nahal Nekarot; to the right of the confluence is the Gev Holit overnight campsite, the starting point of this segment. Above and to the left of the Nahal Kamai channel, the channel of Nahal Geled flows to its waterfall. The adjacent waterfall of Nahal Kamai is hidden. On the skyline, above the Geled waterfall, peek the summits of the Ramon Crater wall, which rise above and east of the Ardon Valley.
The Israel National Trail descends from Har Yahav eastwards into Nahal Tzvira, a tributary of Nahal Nekarot. Rainfall on the eastern slopes of the Negev and in the Arava is less than 50 mm a year. This small amount causes the vegetation to concentrate in the channels and live off the runoff collected from the channel's drainage area.
During the descent, a change in the character of the vegetation is noticeable. In the upper, small channels we generally see low annual plants living off runoff collected from the immediate surroundings. As we descend, several small channels meet to form a larger channel and the composition of plant species in the channel changes, with larger and denser plants. At a certain point acacia trees begin to grow as well.
Two species of acacia grow beside the route: the twisted acacia (Acacia raddiana), like those growing from Mitzpe Ramon to here, and the umbrella thorn acacia (Acacia tortilis), which characterises the lower region (a third species, the Negev acacia, Acacia pachyceras, will appear beside the Israel National Trail in the Shaharut area). An uncertain but simple way to distinguish the two species is by the shape of the tree's crown. The twisted acacia usually has a single trunk that branches out. The umbrella thorn acacia usually has several trunks rising from ground level, and the crown is umbrella-shaped, a flat parasol. A more accurate identification can be made from the leaves and fruits. In the umbrella thorn acacia the leaves and fruits are small and hairy, while in the twisted acacia the leaves are almost entirely hairless and the fruits are large and completely smooth. The umbrella thorn acacia is more drought-resistant and heat-loving; it copes even in relatively small channels, and so it typically characterises elevations of 120 metres and below.
At the confluence of the two tributaries of Nahal Tzvira, the one from which the Israel National Trail arrives and the one into which it turns, we switch to walking along a dirt road climbing gently up the channel. After a short distance, the trail passes through an overnight campsite and continues at the foot of the cliff line to the left of the channel. Where the channel bends right, the trail turns left to the ascent to the top of the cliff, onto the back of the plateau between Nahal Tzvira and Nahal Ashboren. From the top of the ascent there is a view north over Nahal Tzvira.
After crossing the plateau, we see on the left, beyond the edge of the plateau, the basin in which the western tributary of Nahal Ashboren is cutting down. Beside the trail is evidence of a relatively "current" morphological process shaping the landscape and the terrain: a row of cracks in the rock. The forces of erosion are gnawing at the plateau and widening the channel beneath it.
After the descent to the eastern tributary of Nahal Ashboren, the trail winds between several small channels until it turns south up a channel through which we climb gently and cross the watershed between Nahal Ashboren and Nahal Karkashet. It is worth using the acacia trees growing in the channel for a rest in the shade.
The trail passes through gentle terrain, surrounded by expanses of dark stones covering the ground and scattered acacia trees. When we reach a wide valley we can notice the slightly different hue of the surrounding hills: yellow, brown and grey. These hills are made of volcanic ash mixed with sand. Geologists explain that the valley and the hills around it are a "caldera" (the name means a large cauldron in Spanish). This is a term describing a geological event in which a volcano collapsed into the vent from which lava and volcanic ash had been ejected. Further evidence of the volcanic events that took place in the area is a long basalt dyke running from the area of the Ein Yahav petrol station westwards, through Nahal Karkashet, to the area of Nahal Ashboren.
We walk along the edge of the valley to a saddle in the line of hills closing off the valley to the east. A short distance after the trail descends the far side of the saddle, it joins a red-marked dirt road and after another short distance reaches a junction of roads. The Israel National Trail continues south with the red-marked road, while a blue-marked road turns left towards the village of Sapir. The road goes around the village to the south, outside the fence surrounding it, to the entrance gate on the eastern side of the village, the end point of this segment.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
